description:
We are Ares Base Guardians a passionate, multidisciplinary team driven by space exploration, inclusive education, and open science. Our team combines system engineering, AI data integration, and creative pedagogical design to build immersive tools that bridge complex aerospace challenges with young learners.

Our Project: Mission Sol-4: Ares Base Guardians: We developed "Mission Sol-4", a 100% front-end, zero-login educational web game designed for children and educators.
summary: Mission Sol-4: Guardians of Ares Base is an interactive, zero-login, 100% front-end educational web game designed for children aged 7 to 12. Across four Martian Sols at Jezero Crater, players apply the Scientific Method to rescue mission mascot Commander Quack from mounting crises. The project directly addresses the challenge by bridging open NASA science with elementary classrooms. It features progressive age adaptations, dynamic mascot reactions, and a local anti-spoiler pedagogical assistant. Powered by verified NASA data feeds—including CCMC DONKI solar flares, OSDR microbial biofilmes, Mars 2020 Perseverance MEDA weather telemetry, and APOD space imagery—the simulation guarantees full offline resilience via a custom circuit-breaker architecture and native WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility (Large Text, High Contrast/Colorblind modes, and Web Speech API audio descriptions), ensuring full inclusion without collecting any personal data (COPPA/LGPD Kids compliant).
details:
Mission Sol-4: Ares Base Guardians is a narrative-driven STEM rescue simulation structured across 5 interactive screens that guide children aged 7 to 12 through the Scientific Method on Mars:

1. Prologue & Crew Setup (Screen 1)
Players meet mission mascot Commander Quack at Jezero Crater and configure their mission before launch. They can play solo or in a team of 2–4 players with NASA-inspired rotating roles (Mission Lead, Science Officer, Comms Officer, Systems Engineer) and select among 3 progressive age profiles (Explorers 7–9, Strategists 10–12, Parents/Teachers). Native WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility controls (♿)—including Large Text, High Contrast/Colorblind patterns, and bilingual Web Speech audio descriptions—are available from the very first click.


Figure 1: Screen 1 — Prologue & Crew Setup featuring progressive age profiles, rotating team roles, and native WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility controls.

2. Engineering Hangar (Screen 2)
Before departing for Mars, players engineer their rescue spacecraft under strict physical constraints: a $100M budget cap and maximum payload mass limits. Players choose orbital trajectories and equip 3 real NASA scientific instrument kits (OSDR Veggie Greenhouse, MEDA Weather Station, and DONKI Solar Shield/Antenna), receiving immediate visual and physical validation when weight or budget limits are exceeded.


Figure 2: Screen 2 — Engineering Hangar enforcing real physical mass and $100M budget trade-offs across NASA scientific instrument kits.

3. Four Tactical Martian Sols & Anti-Spoiler Tutor (Screen 3)

Across four Martian days (Sols), players face escalating real-world space hazards without any "zero-cost" easy answers—every decision involves authentic engineering trade-offs (Crew Health, Base Integrity, Energy, and Science Points):

  • Sol 1: Tackling microbial biofilms in air ducts at -85°C (NASA OSDR & MEDA data).
  • Sol 2: Surviving a Class X8.7 solar flare under budget constraints (NASA CCMC DONKI data).
  • Sol 3: Stabilizing the Veggie greenhouse 16h/day LED cycle during orbital turbulence.
  • Sol 4: Navigating a Jezero Crater dust storm for orbital rendezvous. Throughout every Sol, Commander Quack reacts with 4 dynamic SVG emotional states and offers a local, deterministic anti-spoiler pedagogical chat that guides players with Socratic hints instead of giving away the answer.


Figure 3: Screen 3 — Tactical Martian Sol decision interface showing Commander Quack's dynamic emotional reactions and local anti-spoiler pedagogical guidance.

4. Zero-G Workshop Minigame (Screen 4 — Sol 3 Interactive Challenge)
During Sol 3, players enter a microgravity repair minigame inside the Veggie greenhouse module, retrieving floating tools in Zero-G to restore life-support and botanical systems before the orbital window closes.



Figure 4: Screen 4 — Interactive Zero-G Workshop minigame inside the Veggie greenhouse module during Sol 3.

5. Victory Celebration, Martian Observatory & Real Science Lab (Screen 5)

Upon completing Sol 4, players unlock their Ares Base Guardian Passport with a celebratory stage featuring procedural Mambo Cubano audio synthesis (Web Audio API), live/cached NASA APOD space imagery, an interactive Martian Night Sky Observatory (identifying Deneb and Orion from Jezero Crater), and a Real Science Audit Lab linking every in-game event directly to peer-reviewed NASA datasets.


Figure 5: Screen 5 — Mission completion celebration, NASA APOD imagery integration, Martian Night Sky Observatory, and Real Science Audit Lab.

Benefits & Impact:

Fosters STEM literacy, systems engineering thinking, and scientific reasoning in children without requiring prior space science knowledge, accounts, or adult setup. Works reliably in public schools and low-connectivity areas thanks to offline-first resilience.

Tools, Languages, AI & Technologies:

Built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vite, Web Audio API, and native Web Speech API (window.speechSynthesis). Developed and deployed via Google AI Studio with video localization/captioning assisted by VMEG. 100% client-side SPA with zero backend servers, databases, and PII collected (COPPA & LGPD Kids compliant).

Creative Aspects & Design Choices:

Features a local deterministic Commander Quack chat with 4 dynamic SVG emotional states, strict anti-spoiler enforcement, progressive age adaptation profiles, and native WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility. Resilient offline architecture uses endpoint circuit-breakers and LocalFallback constants.
